title: Quad Canes: How They Work and What to Check Before You Buy
subtitle: A cane with a four-footed base can offer a bit of extra balance support, as long as it fits you and you know its limits.
excerpt: A quad cane has a small base with four rubber-tipped feet instead of a single tip. Here is how it works, what to check before buying, and how to set the height.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Some days the walk from the bedroom to the kitchen feels longer than it used to. Maybe a knee is sore, a hip is stiff, or your balance is not what it was. A regular cane with a single tip is a common first step, but some people want a little more to lean on.

That is where a quad cane comes in. It looks like a standard cane up top, but at the bottom it has a base with four short legs, called prongs. Each prong ends in a rubber tip, and together they give the cane a wider footprint than a single tip.

The base attaches to the bottom of the shaft and adds stability through those four rubber tips, which are called ferrules. Many quad canes also adjust in height. Adjustable canes use shaft sections that slide inside one another, and a locking pin holds the length you choose.

It helps to be clear about what a quad cane cannot do. It is meant for light support and some weight-bearing. It does not offer the stability of a rollator or walker, and it cannot carry a full load from your legs.
Quad canes are also heavier and bulkier than single-tip canes, and they do not fold. If the cane needs to fit in a car trunk, keep that in mind.

items: Height range: Make sure the cane adjusts to fit you. Small steps, such as 1-inch increments, make it easier to get the height right.
A secure lock: A metal locking pin plus an extra locking screw helps hold the height and position in place.
Weight rating: Check the stated limit. A rating such as 250 lb covers the cane itself, not you plus anything you are carrying or leaning on it.
A comfortable handle: A cushioned or ergonomic grip can ease hand and wrist fatigue. It will not cure arthritis or grip weakness.
Left or right hand: A reversible base lets you use the cane in either hand.
Folding or not: Quad canes do not fold. One product below notes that a folding version is sold separately.
Material: Aluminum or carbon fiber is stronger for its weight than hardwood.
Hidden costs: Rubber tips may need replacing, and shipping can add to the price.
Guarantee: Check whether the seller lists a warranty or guarantee, and read what it covers.

Setting It Up and Using It Well

Getting the height right matters. Wrong height is a common fit error. Stand in the shoes you plan to wear with the cane and let your arms hang naturally. The top of the handle should reach your wrist.
Adjustable canes lock in place, so check the pin and the extra screw, if there is one, after every height change.

If you have balance or mobility problems, talk with a clinician about the right cane style and height. One general reference on canes says people with these problems "should consult a medical professional before choosing the style that best suits them" (Wikipedia, "Assistive cane" article).
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A quad cane is a simple tool, but one that fits you can be a helpful extra bit of support. Take your time choosing, get a professional opinion if you can, and enjoy the walk.
